---
title: Keys and Registry
---

A signature is only as meaningful as the binding between a key and a person. Two kinds of key
exist: a dev-mode software key, enough to build and test every other part of the design and
clearly labelled as not proving who signed, and a passkey, which signs only after the signer's
authenticator has verified them. This page covers where keys live, what the registry records and
how the two modes differ. [Biometric Signing](signing.qmd) covers passkeys in depth.


## Dev-Mode Keys

`sib keygen` creates an Ed25519 private key with the `cryptography` library and stores it under
`SIB_HOME` (`~/.sib` unless the variable is set):

```text
$SIB_HOME/dev-keys/alice@example.com#dev-2026-09.pem
```

The file is PKCS#8 PEM without a passphrase, written with mode `0600`. Characters outside
`A-Za-z0-9._@#-` in the key id are replaced with `_` in the file name. Every command that creates
or uses a dev key prints the same line to standard error:

```text
SIB DEV MODE: currently using software-only keys. Signatures only prove possession of the key file, not a verified human.
```

::: {.callout-important}
A dev key proves that whoever signed could read a file. It does not prove a person was present.
Dev mode exists so the rest of the system can be built and tested; enforced mode refuses dev keys
outright.
:::


## Passkeys

`sib enroll --signer alice@example.com` creates a passkey in the signer's authenticator through
the browser and records its public key in the registry with `alg: ES256-webauthn`. The private
key never leaves the authenticator, and every signature requires the authenticator to verify the
user first. What enrollment records, and what it does and does not prove, is on
[Biometric Signing](signing.qmd).


## Key Identifiers

A key id (`kid`) names one enrolled key and appears in every block signed with it. The convention
is the signer id, a `#`, and a label:

```text
alice@example.com#dev-2026-09
alice@example.com#passkey-9188
```

The label distinguishes a person's keys from each other, so a dev key and a passkey can coexist and
either can be rotated. `keygen` derives `dev-<year>-<month>`; `enroll` derives `passkey-` plus the
first two bytes of the credential id. The verifier does not parse the label; it looks the whole
`kid` up in the registry and checks that the registry's signer matches the header's `iss`.


## Enrollment

Enrollment records a public key under a signer id. For a dev key, create and enroll in one step:

```bash
# Create a dev key and enroll it for alice
sib keygen --signer alice@example.com --enroll
```

```text
SIB DEV MODE: currently using software-only keys. Signatures only prove possession of the key file, not a verified human.
dev key created for kid alice@example.com#dev-2026-09
public key: JmbApRbWb-3nVyk_H9vMHMId6bSA_znZfS2_aRnu5Hc
enrolled alice@example.com#dev-2026-09 for alice@example.com in /tmp/sib-doc-blocks/registry.json (dev mode, attestation_verified=false)
```

For a passkey, `sib enroll --signer alice@example.com` opens the enroll page. To enroll a public
key produced elsewhere, give it on the command line:

`--signer ID`
: The signer's stable identifier (e.g., an email address).

`--kid KID`
: The key id, following the convention above. Required with `--public-key`.

`--public-key KEY`
: The raw public key, base64url without padding.

`--alg ALG`
: The signature algorithm of `--public-key` (default: `EdDSA`).

`--dev`
: Mark the key as a dev key. Without it the key is enrolled in enforced mode.

Enrolling a `kid` that already exists is an error; a key is never silently replaced.


## The Registry File

The registry is one JSON file at `$SIB_HOME/registry.json`:

```json
{
  "signers": [
    {
      "signer": "alice@example.com",
      "keys": [
        {
          "kid": "alice@example.com#dev-2026-09",
          "alg": "EdDSA",
          "public_key": "JmbApRbWb-3nVyk_H9vMHMId6bSA_znZfS2_aRnu5Hc",
          "mode": "dev",
          "enrolled_at": "2026-09-13T14:06:30Z",
          "attestation_verified": false,
          "attestation": {},
          "revoked": false
        },
        {
          "kid": "alice@example.com#passkey-9188",
          "alg": "ES256-webauthn",
          "public_key": "pQECAyYgASFYIAme6lzACHBimeQ_-XoqnWCJGkWnolTu63bWExx4t1mZIlggf_dOOJAncBQ8B9jE1koWCovF_qJejGQv_fBEm2QL1oY",
          "mode": "enforced",
          "enrolled_at": "2026-10-05T11:45:20Z",
          "attestation_verified": false,
          "attestation": {"format": "packed", "x5c_present": true, "roots": null},
          "revoked": false,
          "credential_id": "kYjC6VVDjNGdsK9jHcPPariB-AUWC8KDxWLVH-Vp9p4",
          "aaguid": "01020304-0506-0708-0102-030405060708",
          "sign_count": 1,
          "origins": ["http://localhost:7391"],
          "rp_id": "localhost",
          "user_verified_at_enrollment": true,
          "transports": ["internal"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "allowed_aaguids": {
    "01020304-0506-0708-0102-030405060708": "Chromium virtual authenticator (e2e)"
  }
}
```

Each key carries:

`alg`, `public_key`
: What the verifier needs to check a signature: a raw Ed25519 key for `EdDSA`, a COSE-encoded
  P-256 key for `ES256-webauthn`, both base64url. The verifier also requires the header's `alg` to
  match this entry.

`mode`
: `dev` or `enforced`. A key enrolled in dev mode fails with `dev_key_in_enforced_mode` when the
  verifier runs in enforced mode, whatever the block's own header says.

`enrolled_at`
: When the entry was made, RFC 3339 in UTC.

`attestation_verified`, `attestation`
: Whether the enrollment carried attestation that chained to a known root, and what the
  statement contained. Always false and empty for dev keys. This is the field that separates
  "hardware backing verified" from "hardware backing assumed".

`revoked`
: Honored by the verifier (status `revoked`), but no command sets it yet.

`credential_id`, `aaguid`, `sign_count`, `origins`, `rp_id`, `transports`
: The WebAuthn enrollment record; see [What the Registry
  Attests](signing.qmd#what-the-registry-attests).

The optional top-level `allowed_aaguids` adds authenticator models to the built-in
biometric-capable allowlist, as `"<aaguid>": "<label>"`.

The registry is the stand-in for the external directory that maps signer keys to people, which the
project treats as out of scope. It is a flat file so that it stays easy to inspect and to ship with
a demo; it is not access-controlled beyond file permissions.


## Dev Mode and Enforced Mode

The verifier's mode comes from the harness. `SIB_MODE` sets it; when the variable is unset the
mode is `enforced` once any passkey is enrolled in the registry and `dev` before that. The mode is
recorded in every manifest. The two modes differ in three places:

- **Dev keys**: accepted in dev mode, refused in enforced mode.

- **Audience**: a block with no `aud` is accepted in dev mode and is `audience_mismatch` in
  enforced mode.

- **Warnings**: dev mode prints its warning on every operation. Enforced mode is silent.

Nothing else changes: a passkey-signed block runs every check of its path in either mode, so a
session can be developed in dev mode and switched to enforced mode once a passkey is enrolled.
